title: Record consistency under repeated readout and apparatus composition
abstract: No-signalling constraints on isolated outcome probabilities do not determine whether an apparatus preserves the joint law of its accessible records under repeated readout, network composition, or reuse. We study these extensions through a conditional-record criterion and four explicit models. For a wrapped-Cauchy retrocausal source, protection under two conditionally independent continuous readouts forces an angle-independent response; three readouts suffice without continuity. A finite angular-bandwidth assumption gives a quantitative leakage bound, whereas continuity alone gives no uniform stability. At a specified two-source Bell junction, the required correction matrix has full nonnegative rank on every even uniform angular grid. A Gaussian controller can cancel branch-mass dependence while leaving a distinguishable joint record, for which we derive exact noise and law-change tradeoffs. Finally, a fixed singlet with shared classical noise reproduces the variable-width isolated outcome family, but retained and refreshed controllers generate different temporal statistics. We prove a finite-resource obstruction and construct positive finite-controller approximations. Numerical studies comprising 8.3 million independent simulated histories support the model-specific predictions. Together, the results identify conditions that must accompany marginal no-signalling when extending an apparatus to richer records and interventions.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the robustness of no-signalling constraints when an experimental apparatus is extended through repeated measurements or network connections. Using advanced mathematical tools, the authors establish necessary conditions—beyond simple marginal constraints—that must hold for the joint record law to remain consistent. The findings provide a detailed framework for understanding the limitations of local realism in complex measurement settings.
main_problem: The paper investigates the necessary conditions for an apparatus to maintain the joint law of its accessible records when subjected to complex extensions like repeated readout, network composition, or reuse, even if initial isolated outcome probabilities satisfy no-signalling constraints.
main_result: The study derives specific, non-trivial conditions—such as angle-independent responses for two readouts or full non-negative rank for correction matrices—that must accompany marginal no-signalling when extending an apparatus to richer records.
method: The authors employ a conditional-record criterion, utilizing tools from Fourier analysis, total variation distance bounds, and developing four explicit mathematical models to test these extensions.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on retrocausal models, specifically using a wrapped-Cauchy retrocausal source and developing criteria for apparatus extension across different measurement scenarios (e.g., Bell junctions, continuous readouts).
key_observables: Joint record distribution, total variation distance ($L_2$), detector response function ($f$), and the rank of required correction matrices.
important_parameters: Angular bandwidth ($\gamma$), the number of readouts (two vs. three), and the resource constraints of the controller.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on defining accessible records, assuming fixed preparation/interventions, and distinguishing between passive readouts and active interventions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the finite-error behavior of smooth responses for two and three readouts, and compare single-readout probabilities versus joint probabilities for different detector types.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the source/apparatus specification, then detailing the conditional-record criterion, and finally applying this criterion to four distinct extension scenarios: repeated readout, network composition, and variable-width source laws.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical constraints on how local no-signalling principles must be extended to describe complex, multi-stage quantum or retrocausal measurements, which has implications for understanding measurement theory beyond simple Bell tests.
